results.content:
Notch rescue tray: catches icons trapped behind the MacBook camera notch in a compact dropdown tray centered right under the notch so you can click them in place, then close it with a click or a two-finger swipe up

   Record a Pin: click "Record a Pin...", click any item in another app's menu bar menu once, and save that single command with its app icon and its own global hotkey while the app's menu bar icon stays hidden.

   New Arrivals: newly installed menu bar apps start out hidden by default, and Hemmed lights a quiet coral dot on its glyph upon arrival. Click the Hemmed glyph to choose Make Visible or Keep Hidden. [...] Hungry Icons: on battery power, when hidden or tray-rescued menu bar apps use high energy, Hemmed shows a silent compact leaf-and-count pill (🍃 N) beside the glyph, badges those icons in the tray, and offers a one-click "Quit the hungry ones" action

   Same Bar on Every Mac: Hemmed syncs your menu bar layout across your Macs through iCloud automatically, including hidden/visible state, icon order, Pinned Actions, and preferences (requires being signed into iCloud)

Hemmed is a native Swift app for macOS 13 or later. It is $14.99 paid once (up to 3 Macs per license), with a 14-day free trial and a 30-day refund window.

# Fix the Notch: How to Stop macOS Hiding Your Menu Bar Icons

The notch on modern MacBooks gives us beautiful, near-borderless displays. But for heavy multitaskers, it introduces a frustrating design flaw: macOS hides menu bar icons behind the notch when you run out of space. Because Apple provides no native overflow menu, essential utility apps simply disappear into a digital black hole. You shouldn't have to force-quit applications just to access your status icons.

Here is how to quickly reclaim your MacBook menu bar real estate.

## 1. Condense Everything with "Only Switch" (Free & Open Source) [...] If your menu bar is cluttered with individual icons for Dark Mode, Keep Awake, Bluetooth, and Night Shift, you are wasting prime real estate.

Only Switch is a powerful, open-source utility that consolidates dozens of settings into a single menu bar icon. Clicking it reveals a clean dropdown panel of customizable toggles. By replacing five or six separate app icons with just one, you instantly clear massive space so other apps never get pushed behind the notch.

## 2. Hide Clutter with a Menu Bar Manager

If you have a large collection of apps that need to stay running, use a dedicated manager to collapse them into a hidden drawer.

`Command (⌘)`

## 3. Tighten Icon Spacing via Terminal (No Apps Required) [...] ## 3. Tighten Icon Spacing via Terminal (No Apps Required)

Apple quietly increased the horizontal padding between menu bar icons in recent macOS versions, wasting valuable screen width. You can force macOS to tighten this spacing using two quick Terminal commands:

`Cmd + Space`
`defaults write com.apple.controlcenter "NSStatusItem2ExtensionMinPadding" -int 6`
`defaults write com.apple.controlcenter "NSStatusItemSpacing" -int 6`
`killall ControlCenter`

To revert to Apple's default airy spacing, run the same commands but change `-int 6` to `-int 12`.

`-int 6`
`-int 12`

results.title: How to Declutter the Mac Menu Bar in macOS Tahoe - OS X Daily
results.content:
A good rule of thumb for managing the Mac menu bar is to hide anything you don’t need constant or quick access to, especially if you can access it from the Control Center (which in itself, is yet another menu bar item). So things like Bluetooth toggles, sound levels, Time Machine, screen mirroring, Focus mode, you might consider hiding, and instead relying on accessing those items through Control Center instead. I also hide the majority of unnecessary third party tools from my menu bar, since it seems like just about every tool and app nowadays wants to install a menu bar item.

Be selective, disable and remove anything you don’t use frequently, and if you rarely use it, you’ll almost certainly want to hide it. [...] Fortunately the latest versions of MacOS give the user some options to declutter the menu bar and remove and hide icons easily, allowing you to quickly improve your menu bar experience.

## How to Declutter Mac Menu Bar with System Settings

On modern MacOS versions like Tahoe, there’s now a dedicated “Menu Bar” section of System Settings where you can manage visibility of menu bar items and tools:

1. Go to  Apple menu and choose “System Settings”
2. Go to “Menu Bar”
3. Scroll down and look below Menu Bar Controls, and toggle the checkbox off for any menu bar items you do not use, do not need, or might otherwise not find useful [...] ### Still overwhelmed? 3rd party tools can hide and show menu bar items on Mac

Another option is to use third party utilities that can hide menu bar items, usually that place them behind an expandable icon. The idea is pretty simple; all the icons you don’t always want visible will tuck behind an arrow, to which you click and then the icons temporarily expand out of.

There are a variety of options available to perform this function, including the free tool like Vanilla to hide and show menu bar icons, or paid apps like Bartender that offer similar features.

results.title: macOS Tahoe Makes it Extremely Easy to Clean Up a Messy Menu Bar
results.content:
Over the years, my Mac’s menu bar has been littered with a slew of menu bar icons. They seem to multiply, like Tribbles. And, like most Mac users, I’ve used third party tools like Ice and Bartender to manage them. While it felt good to sweep menu bar icons “under the rug” by hiding them from view, it never felt quite right. I also found myself wondering what some of the menu bar items were. (It would be nice to have the option to view the name of the menu bar item by hovering your Mac’s cursor over it, but I digress…)

Why?

Because, in my day-to-day work, I use but a handful of menu bar icons on a regular basis. With that in mind, I conducted my own internal audit to decide what menu bar items should stay and what should go.
